items.question: In Activity 12.7, when the direction of current in rod AB is reversed, what happens to the displacement of the rod?

options.A: Rod stays in the same position
options.B: Rod moves in the same direction with more force
options.C: Rod moves in the opposite direction

items.explanation: When the direction of current is reversed, the direction of the force on the rod (and hence its displacement) is reversed. This was observed in Activity 12.7 when cell connections were changed.

items.question: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is maximum when the current is at what angle to the field?
items.explanation: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is maximum when the direction of current is at RIGHT ANGLES (90 degrees) to the direction of the magnetic field. At 0 degrees (parallel), the force is zero.

items.question: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the forefinger represent?
items.explanation: In Fleming's left-hand rule: FOREFINGER = direction of MAGNETIC FIELD (B), MIDDLE FINGER = direction of CURRENT (I), and THUMB = direction of FORCE/MOTION (F). Remember: FBI (Force, B-field, I-current) with thumb-forefinger-middle finger.

items.question: Which of the following devices works on the principle of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?
items.explanation: An electric motor uses the principle of force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field to produce rotational motion (converts electrical energy to mechanical energy). Loudspeakers, microphones, and galvanometers also use this principle.

items.question: An electron moving towards the east is deflected towards the south by a magnetic field. In which direction is the magnetic field acting?
items.explanation: Electron moves EAST, force is towards SOUTH. Note: conventional current is OPPOSITE to electron motion, so current direction = WEST. Apply Fleming's left-hand rule: Middle finger = WEST (current), Thumb = SOUTH (force). Forefinger = UPWARD (field direction). Magnetic field is directed UPWARD.

items.question: In Activity 12.7, if both the direction of current AND the direction of magnetic field are reversed simultaneously, what happens to the displacement of rod AB?

options.B: Displacement in the SAME direction as original

items.explanation: By Fleming's left-hand rule, reversing only the current reverses the force direction; reversing only the field also reverses the force direction. But reversing BOTH current and field simultaneously means the force direction changes twice (reverses twice), bringing it back to the ORIGINAL direction. So displacement remains in the same direction.

items.question: Which property of a proton DOES NOT change when it moves freely in a uniform magnetic field?
items.explanation: A magnetic force acts PERPENDICULAR to the velocity of a moving charge. This changes the DIRECTION of motion (hence velocity and momentum, both vectors, change). However, since the force is always perpendicular to motion, it does NO WORK on the particle, so the SPEED (magnitude of velocity) remains constant.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: DOMESTIC ELECTRIC CIRCUIT: The system of wiring and distribution used to supply electrical power from the main supply to various appliances in our homes is called a DOMESTIC ELECTRIC CIRCUIT. In our homes, we receive ALTERNATING CURRENT (AC) supply at 220 V and frequency 50 Hz.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Electric power is received in homes through a MAIN SUPPLY (also called mains) either through overhead electric poles or underground cables.
There are THREE WIRES in the domestic supply:
1. LIVE WIRE (positive wire): Has red insulation cover. Carries current into the circuit.
2. NEUTRAL WIRE (negative wire): Has black insulation cover.
3. EARTH WIRE: Has green insulation cover. Connected to a metallic plate buried deep in the earth near the house. Used as a safety measure.
The potential difference between live and neutral wires = 220 V.
These wires pass into the house through an ELECTRICITY BOARD'S FUSE and then an ELECTRICITY METER, then through a MAIN SWITCH and DISTRIBUTION BOX.
Two separate circuits in domestic supply:
1. 15 A CIRCUIT: For appliances with higher power ratings (geysers, air conditioners, etc.)
2. 5 A CIRCUIT: For bulbs, fans, etc.
All domestic appliances are connected in PARALLEL across the live and neutral wires.
Each appliance has a separate switch to allow independent ON/OFF control.

ELECTRIC FUSE: An important safety device. Prevents damage to appliances and circuits from overloading and short-circuiting. Works by Joule heating - when excess current flows, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit.
OVERLOADING: Can occur when the live wire and neutral wire come into direct contact (short circuit) or when too many appliances are connected to a single socket.

SHORT CIRCUIT: Occurs when the insulation of wires is damaged or a fault in the appliance causes the live wire and neutral wire to come into direct contact. The current in the circuit abruptly increases.

EARTH WIRE: Connected to the metallic body of appliances. Provides a low-resistance path for current if there is any leakage. Ensures leakage current flows to earth and keeps the potential of the metallic body at earth potential, protecting users from severe electric shock.
In our country, we receive AC electric power of 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.
QUESTIONS (Textbook after 12.4):
1. Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
A: Two safety measures commonly used are:
(i) ELECTRIC FUSE: Placed in series in the circuit. When excess current flows (due to short circuit or overloading), the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, preventing damage.

(ii) EARTH WIRE (Earthing): The metallic bodies of appliances are connected to the earth wire. If there is any leakage of current to the metallic body, it flows safely to the earth, preventing electric shock to the user.
2. An electric oven of 2 kW power rating is operated in a domestic electric circuit (220 V) that has a current rating of 5 A. What result do you expect? Explain.
A: CALCULATION:
Power of oven = 2 kW = 2000 W
Voltage = 220 V
Current drawn by oven = P/V = 2000/220 = 9.09 A
Since the oven draws about 9.09 A, which is GREATER than the current rating of the circuit (5 A), the circuit will be OVERLOADED.
RESULT: The fuse of the 5 A circuit will BLOW (melt) due to overloading. The circuit will be broken, and the oven will not operate. The oven should be used on the 15 A circuit instead.
3. What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
A: Precautions to avoid overloading:
(i) Do not connect too many appliances to a single socket or circuit.
(ii) Ensure the total current demand of all appliances connected to a circuit does not exceed the rated current of that circuit.
(iii) Use the correct circuit (15 A for high-power appliances; 5 A for lights and fans).
(iv) Do not use damaged or worn-out wires with broken insulation.
(v) Ensure the correct rating fuse is used in each circuit.

items.question: Name the three wires in the domestic electric supply. Give their insulation colours.
items.answer:
The three wires in domestic electric supply are:
1. LIVE WIRE: Insulated with RED cover. This is the positive wire that carries current from the supply.
2. NEUTRAL WIRE: Insulated with BLACK cover. This is the negative wire.
3. EARTH WIRE: Insulated with GREEN cover. Connected to a metallic plate buried in the earth. Used as a safety measure to prevent electric shock.

items.question: Why are domestic appliances connected in parallel and not in series?
items.answer:
Domestic appliances are connected in PARALLEL (across the live and neutral wires) and not in series for the following reasons:
1. In parallel connection, each appliance gets the FULL 220 V supply. In series, voltage would be divided among appliances, making them work poorly.
2. Each appliance can be SWITCHED ON OR OFF INDEPENDENTLY without affecting others. In series, switching off one device would disconnect all others.
3. If one appliance fails, the others continue to work normally.

items.question: What is a fuse? Why is it important in domestic circuits? How does it work?
items.answer:
FUSE: An electric fuse is an important safety device used in domestic circuits to prevent damage to appliances and wiring from overloading and short-circuiting.

IMPORTANCE: A fuse is connected in SERIES in the circuit. It prevents excessive current from flowing through the circuit, which would otherwise overheat and damage the wiring and appliances.

HOW IT WORKS (Based on Joule Heating):
- The fuse wire is made of a material with a LOW MELTING POINT.
- Under normal conditions, current flows through the fuse without melting it.
- When the current exceeds the safe limit (due to overloading or short circuit), the JOULE HEATING produced in the fuse wire becomes very high.
- This heat MELTS the fuse wire, BREAKING the circuit.
- The broken circuit stops the flow of current, protecting the appliances.
- The fuse must be replaced after it melts before the circuit can be used again.

items.question: What is short-circuiting? What is overloading? How do fuses protect against these?
items.answer:
SHORT CIRCUIT:
A SHORT CIRCUIT occurs when the live wire and the neutral wire come into DIRECT CONTACT with each other (without passing through an appliance). This happens when:
- The insulation of wires is damaged or worn out.
- There is a fault inside an appliance.
Effect: At the point of short circuit, there is ZERO or very low resistance. By Ohm's law (I = V/R), the current increases DRASTICALLY and abruptly. This very high current can cause overheating, sparks, and fire.

OVERLOADING:
OVERLOADING occurs when the total current drawn by all appliances connected in a circuit exceeds the rated (safe) current of the circuit. This can happen when:
- Too many appliances are connected to a single socket or circuit simultaneously.
- An accidental hike in supply voltage occurs.
Effect: Excessive current flows, causing overheating of wires.

HOW FUSES PROTECT:
- Fuses are connected IN SERIES in the circuit.
- Each circuit has a fuse rated for its maximum safe current (e.g., 5 A for lighting circuit, 15 A for power circuit).
- In both short circuit and overloading situations, the current exceeds the fuse rating.
- The Joule heating in the fuse wire melts it, BREAKING THE CIRCUIT and stopping the current flow.
- This prevents damage to appliances, wiring, and prevents fire hazards.

items.question: Explain the role of the earth wire in domestic electric supply. Why is earthing necessary for metallic appliances?
items.answer:
EARTH WIRE:
The EARTH WIRE is the third wire in our domestic supply. It is covered with GREEN insulation and is connected to a METALLIC PLATE buried deep in the earth near the house.

ROLE IN DOMESTIC CIRCUITS:
1. The earth wire is connected to the METALLIC BODIES of all electrical appliances (electric press, toaster, table fan, refrigerator, etc.).
2. Under normal conditions, no current flows through the earth wire.
3. If there is any LEAKAGE OF CURRENT to the metallic body of an appliance (due to damaged insulation inside), the leakage current flows THROUGH THE EARTH WIRE to the ground.
4. The earth wire provides a LOW-RESISTANCE PATH for leakage current.

WHY EARTHING IS NECESSARY:
1. SAFETY FROM ELECTRIC SHOCK: Without earthing, if leakage current reaches the metallic body of an appliance, the potential of the body rises. A person touching it would receive a SEVERE ELECTRIC SHOCK (current would flow through the body to ground).
2. With earthing, the leakage current flows safely to the earth, keeping the metallic body at EARTH POTENTIAL (zero potential). A person touching it is safe as no significant current flows through them.
3. FIRE PREVENTION: Continuous leakage without earthing could cause overheating and fire; earthing prevents this.
4. Earthing is MANDATORY for all metallic appliances as per safety regulations.

items.question: Describe the domestic electric circuit in a house. Include the components, types of circuits, safety measures, and the role of each wire.
items.answer:
DOMESTIC ELECTRIC CIRCUIT:

POWER SUPPLY:
Homes receive ALTERNATING CURRENT (AC) at 220 V, 50 Hz frequency from the electric power company, either through overhead cables or underground lines.

THE THREE WIRES:
1. LIVE WIRE (red insulation): Carries the 220 V supply into the house from the main supply.
2. NEUTRAL WIRE (black insulation): Acts as the return wire.
3. EARTH WIRE (green insulation): Safety wire connected to a metallic plate buried in earth.
The potential difference between live and neutral = 220 V.

ENTRY INTO HOUSE:
The wires enter through: ELECTRICITY BOARD'S FUSE → ELECTRICITY METER (records consumption) → MAIN SWITCH → DISTRIBUTION BOX (contains fuses for separate circuits).

TWO TYPES OF CIRCUITS:
1. 15 A CIRCUIT: For high-power appliances like geysers, air conditioners, heaters. Wires with 15 A current rating.
2. 5 A CIRCUIT: For lights, fans, TVs, etc. Wires with 5 A current rating.

PARALLEL CONNECTION:
All appliances are connected in PARALLEL across the live and neutral wires. Each has its own switch. Benefits: each gets full 220 V; independent ON/OFF; failure of one doesn't affect others.

SAFETY MEASURES:
1. ELECTRIC FUSE: Connected in series in each circuit. Made of material with low melting point. Melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds safe limit (due to overloading or short circuit). Based on Joule heating principle.

2. EARTH WIRE: Connected to metallic bodies of appliances. If leakage occurs, current flows safely to ground instead of through a person's body. Prevents electric shock.

FAULTS IN CIRCUIT:
- SHORT CIRCUIT: Live and neutral wires make direct contact → very high current → fuse blows.
- OVERLOADING: Too many appliances → current exceeds limit → fuse blows.
- In both cases, the fuse prevents damage.

CIRCUIT DIAGRAM DESCRIPTION:
Main supply → Board's fuse → Meter → Main switch → Distribution box → Two branches: (i) 15 A circuit to high-power appliances; (ii) 5 A circuit to lights and fans. Earth wire connected to all metallic appliance bodies. All appliances in parallel (Fig. 12.15).

options.C: Between live and earth wires only

items.explanation: In India, domestic electric supply is at 220 V alternating current (AC) with a frequency of 50 Hz. The potential difference between the live wire and the neutral wire is 220 V.

items.question: Why is the earth wire connected to the metallic body of appliances like electric presses and refrigerators?

options.A: To increase the efficiency of the appliance
options.B: To provide extra current to the appliance
options.C: To ensure leakage current flows safely to the earth, preventing electric shock
options.D: To reduce the voltage supplied to the appliance

items.explanation: The earth wire provides a low-resistance path for any leakage current to flow safely to the earth (ground). This keeps the metallic body of the appliance at earth potential, preventing a user from getting a severe electric shock on touching the metallic body.

items.question: At the time of a short circuit, the current in the circuit:
items.explanation: In a short circuit, the live and neutral wires come into direct contact (very low resistance path). By Ohm's law (I = V/R), since R ≈ 0, the current increases very heavily/abruptly. This is why the fuse melts quickly during a short circuit.

items.question: An electric appliance of 1100 W is connected to a 220 V domestic supply. The fuse used in the circuit has a rating of 5 A. What will happen?

options.B: The fuse will blow as the appliance draws more than 5 A
options.C: The voltage will drop to 110 V
options.D: The appliance will only receive 5 A and function partially

items.explanation: Current drawn = P/V = 1100/220 = 5 A. The current drawn is EXACTLY 5 A, which equals the fuse rating. The fuse will NOT blow; the appliance works normally (a fuse typically blows when the current significantly exceeds its rating, not at exactly the rated value).

items.question: A house has two circuits: a 5 A lighting circuit and a 15 A power circuit. A 2000 W geyser (220 V) is accidentally connected to the 5 A lighting circuit. What will happen and why?

options.A: Geyser will work normally as 220 V is available
options.B: The 5 A fuse will blow because the geyser draws about 9.1 A
options.C: The 15 A fuse will blow instead

items.explanation: Current drawn by geyser = P/V = 2000/220 ≈ 9.1 A. The 5 A fuse in the lighting circuit will BLOW because 9.1 A exceeds its 5 A rating. The geyser should be connected to the 15 A power circuit which can safely handle this current.

sections.label: WHAT YOU HAVE LEARNT:
sections.text:
- A compass needle is a small magnet. Its one end, which points towards north, is called a north pole, and the other end, which points towards south, is called a south pole.
- A magnetic field exists in the region surrounding a magnet, in which the force of the magnet can be detected.
- Field lines are used to represent a magnetic field. A field line is the path along which a hypothetical free north pole would tend to move. The direction of the magnetic field at a point is given by the direction that a north pole placed at that point would take. Field lines are shown closer together where the magnetic field is greater.
- A metallic wire carrying an electric current has associated with it a magnetic field. The field lines about the wire consist of a series of concentric circles whose direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule.
- The pattern of the magnetic field around a conductor due to an electric current flowing through it depends on the shape of the conductor. The magnetic field of a solenoid carrying a current is similar to that of a bar magnet.
- An electromagnet consists of a core of soft iron wrapped around with a coil of insulated copper wire.
- A current-carrying conductor when placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. If the direction of the field and that of the current are mutually perpendicular to each other, then the force acting on the conductor will be perpendicular to both and will be given by Fleming's left-hand rule. This is the basis of an electric motor.
- In our houses, we receive AC electric power of 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz. One of the wires in this supply is with red insulation, called live wire. The other one is of black insulation, which is a neutral wire. The potential difference between the two is 220 V. The third is the earth wire that has green insulation and this is connected to a metallic body deep inside earth. It is used as a safety measure to ensure that any leakage of current to a metallic body does not give any severe shock to a user.
- Fuse is the most important safety device, used for protecting the circuits due to short-circuiting or overloading of the circuits.

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.1:

(a) The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire.
(b) The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire.
(c) The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire.
(d) The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
A: (d) The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.2:
sections.raw:
Q: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit
(a) reduces substantially.
(b) does not change.
(c) increases heavily.
(d) vary continuously.
A: (c) increases heavily.

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.3:
sections.raw:
Q: State whether the following statements are true or false.
(a) The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines.
(b) A wire with a green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
A: (a) TRUE - At the centre of a circular coil, field lines appear as parallel straight lines.
(b) FALSE - The wire with GREEN insulation is the EARTH wire, not the live wire. The LIVE wire has RED insulation.

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.4:
sections.raw:
Q: List two methods of producing magnetic fields.
A: Two methods of producing magnetic fields:
1. Using a PERMANENT MAGNET (a bar magnet, horseshoe magnet, etc. naturally produces a magnetic field around it).
2. By passing ELECTRIC CURRENT through a conductor (the magnetic effect of electric current produces a field around any current-carrying conductor, wire, coil, or solenoid).

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.5:
sections.raw:
Q: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
A: The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field is LARGEST when the direction of the current is at RIGHT ANGLES (perpendicular, 90 degrees) to the direction of the magnetic field. At this angle, the force is maximum = BIL (where B = field strength, I = current, L = length of conductor). When current is parallel to the field (0 degrees), the force is ZERO.

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.6:
sections.raw:
Q: Imagine that you are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam, moving horizontally from back wall towards the front wall, is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of magnetic field?
A: The electron beam moves HORIZONTALLY from back to front (let's say this is towards the NORTH direction). The electrons are deflected towards the RIGHT (EAST).

Since electrons have negative charge, conventional current direction is OPPOSITE to electron motion, i.e., current flows from FRONT to BACK (SOUTHWARD).

Applying FLEMING'S LEFT-HAND RULE:
- Middle finger (current): pointing SOUTH (towards back wall).
- Thumb (force on electrons): pointing EAST (towards right).
- Forefinger (magnetic field): must be pointing VERTICALLY DOWNWARD.

ANSWER: The direction of the magnetic field is VERTICALLY DOWNWARD.

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.7:
sections.raw:
Q: State the rule to determine the direction of a (i) magnetic field produced around a straight conductor-carrying current, (ii) force experienced by a current-carrying straight conductor placed in a magnetic field which is perpendicular to it.
A: (i) MAGNETIC FIELD AROUND STRAIGHT CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR:
RIGHT-HAND THUMB RULE (Maxwell's Corkscrew Rule): Imagine holding the current-carrying straight conductor in the right hand such that the THUMB points in the direction of the current. Then, the FINGERS curling around the conductor give the direction of the magnetic field lines around the conductor.

(ii) FORCE ON CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR IN MAGNETIC FIELD (perpendicular):
FLEMING'S LEFT-HAND RULE: Stretch the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger of the LEFT HAND mutually perpendicular. If the FOREFINGER points in the direction of the MAGNETIC FIELD and the MIDDLE FINGER points in the direction of the CURRENT, then the THUMB points in the direction of the FORCE (motion) acting on the conductor.

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.8:
sections.raw:
Q: When does an electric short circuit occur?
A: An electric SHORT CIRCUIT occurs when the LIVE WIRE and the NEUTRAL WIRE come into DIRECT CONTACT with each other. This can happen when:
1. The INSULATION of the wires is damaged (worn out, cut, or melted due to excessive heat).
2. There is a FAULT inside the electrical appliance.
Effect: At the point of contact, the resistance is nearly zero. By Ohm's law (I = V/R), the current increases abruptly to a very high value. This can cause overheating, sparks, fire, and damage to appliances. The fuse in the circuit should melt to break the circuit and prevent further damage.

sections.label: EXERCISE 12.9:
sections.raw:
Q: What is the function of an earth wire? Why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
A: FUNCTION OF EARTH WIRE:
The earth wire (green insulation) is connected to a metallic plate buried deep in the earth near the house. It is also connected to the metallic bodies of electrical appliances.

FUNCTION: If there is any leakage of current to the metallic body of an appliance (due to damaged insulation or internal fault), the earth wire provides a LOW-RESISTANCE PATH for the leakage current to flow SAFELY to the earth (ground) instead of through a person's body.

WHY NECESSARY TO EARTH METALLIC APPLIANCES:
1. PREVENTION OF ELECTRIC SHOCK: Without earthing, if leakage current reaches the metallic body, the body acquires a high potential. A person touching it would receive a SEVERE ELECTRIC SHOCK (current would flow through the body, which is dangerous or even fatal).
2. With earthing, the metallic body is maintained at EARTH POTENTIAL (zero). A person touching it is safe.
3. PROTECTION OF APPLIANCES: Earthing ensures any leakage current flows harmlessly to earth, preventing damage.
4. Metallic appliances like electric press (iron), toaster, table fan, refrigerator, etc. MUST be earthed as they have conducting bodies that users regularly touch.
